title: More than seven in ten lung cancers diagnosed late as Northern Ireland screening plans face uncertain timetable
text:
More than seven in ten lung cancers diagnosed late as Northern Ireland screening plans face uncertain timetable Love Ballymena

ARTICLE PAGE TEXT:
(L-R) Sisters Nuala, Sinead, Ciara and Emma who took part in Race for Life in memory of their mum Margaret Cusack who died from lung cancer.
More than seven in ten lung cancer cases in Northern Ireland are diagnosed at an advanced stage, according to Cancer Research UK , as the Health Minister confirms that planning for a targeted screening programme is being funded but cannot say when it will become available to patients.
The charity's analysis found that 71% of lung cancer cases with a known stage were diagnosed at stages three or four between 2018 and 2022, when treatment is less likely to be successful.
Around 1,300 people are diagnosed with lung cancer in Northern Ireland each year, according to the Public Health Agency (PHA).
Health Minister Robbie Butler told the Northern Ireland Assembly on 10 November that his department had provided funding to the PHA to establish a project team and begin planning targeted screening.
The work is expected to take approximately 12 months, with full implementation likely to require substantial additional investment.
The announcement comes during Lung Cancer Awareness Month, with Cancer Research UK calling for urgent action and the PHA encouraging people to recognise symptoms that could indicate the disease.
Speaking at Stormont, Mr Butler acknowledged that Northern Ireland does not currently have a targeted lung cancer screening programme and expressed regret that one was not already available.
He confirmed that the PHA would develop a regional plan covering screening, additional diagnostic services, follow-up investigations and treatment pathways.
The estimated annual cost of a fully implemented programme is approximately £9 million, although the Minister warned that development and implementation costs could be significantly higher because Northern Ireland is starting from a different position than England.
“At this stage, I am unable to outline a specific time frame for the full implementation of a lung cancer screening programme in Northern Ireland.”
The position represents a change from the December 2024 health and social care plan, which had envisaged introducing targeted lung screening by April 2027, subject to additional funding.
Planning is now expected to begin in December 2026 and take around a year, with no confirmed date for patients to begin receiving screening invitations.
The UK National Screening Committee recommended in 2022 that targeted screening be introduced across all four UK nations for people aged 55 to 74 at higher risk of developing lung cancer, including current and former smokers. Screening uses low-dose CT scans to help detect lung cancer before symptoms develop.
England has begun rolling out screening, while Scotland is planning phased implementation and Wales expects its first invitations under a wider programme in 2028.
Cancer Research UK says the difference in survival between early and advanced lung cancer demonstrates the importance of detecting the disease sooner.
In Northern Ireland, 52% of people diagnosed at stage one survive for at least five years, compared with just 2% of those diagnosed at stage four.
Lung cancer remains Northern Ireland's biggest cancer killer, with Cancer Research UK citing approximately 980 deaths annually.
The charity estimates that a fully implemented screening programme could save around 70 lives every year if 60% of eligible people accepted an invitation. It also projects wider economic benefits of approximately £45 million annually. These are estimates rather than outcomes already achieved.
Liz Morrison, Cancer Research UK's public affairs manager in Northern Ireland , said:
“Far too many people in Northern Ireland are being diagnosed with lung cancer at a late stage when there are fewer treatment options.
